opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

The biggest difference is that AlphaFold 1 was a pipeline and AlphaFold 2 is a single model you train end to end. In AlphaFold 1 we had a neural network predict distograms, which are probability distributions over distances between pairs of residues. Then a separate step took those distributions, turned them into a potential, and ran gradient descent on the structure to find something consistent with them. That worked surprisingly well, and it won CASP13. But the network never saw the final structure. It was trained to get the distances right, and then something else entirely had to work out the geometry.

In AlphaFold 2 we asked what happens if the network reasons about the structure directly and is trained on the thing we actually care about, the 3D coordinates. Several architectural ideas came out of taking that seriously.

The first is the Evoformer. Rather than squeezing the multiple sequence alignment into hand-built features up front, we keep a representation of the MSA and a pairwise representation of residue relationships, and they talk to each other over many layers. The MSA side looks at evolutionary information, things like which positions co-vary, and writes that into the pair representation. The pair representation in turn biases attention over the MSA. So the network gets to decide what evolutionary signal matters, instead of us deciding for it.

The second is the triangle updates. If you think of the pair representation as edges in a graph of residues, then geometric consistency is about triangles: if I know something about i to j and j to k, that constrains i to k. Building that inductive bias in, through triangle multiplicative updates and triangle attention, was one of those things that looked a bit odd on paper and turned out to matter a great deal in the ablations.

The third is the structure module. It works directly on residues as rigid frames, with a rotation and translation for each one, and uses invariant point attention, so the geometry is handled in a way that respects 3D rotations and translations. We train it with a loss on the structure itself, the frame-aligned point error, so gradients come all the way back from the atomic positions.

Then there's a set of things that are less glamorous and, to be honest, just as important. Recycling feeds the model's own output back in so it can refine its answer over several passes. Self-distillation on predicted structures for sequences without solved structures gave us a lot more training signal. Masked MSA prediction acts as an auxiliary objective. And the model predicts its own confidence through pLDDT, which turned out to be enormously useful to the biologists actually using it.

What I'd like people to take from this is that no single trick did it. When we ablated the system, a lot of components each contributed something meaningful. The real advance was moving from "predict some features, then hand off to an optimizer" to "build a network whose structure reflects the geometry and evolution of the problem, and train it end to end on what you actually want." That's what got us from a good CASP13 result to accuracy that was often competitive with experiment at CASP14.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that AlphaFold 1 was, in a sense, a very good version of the old approach, and AlphaFold 2 was a different approach altogether. AlphaFold 1 took the multiple sequence alignment, ran it through a fairly conventional residual convolutional network, and predicted a distogram, a set of pairwise distances. Then we handed that off to a separate gradient descent procedure that tried to find a structure consistent with those distances. So the neural network never actually saw a protein structure. It saw statistics about a protein structure. And once it produced its distance map, that was it. There was no way for it to look at the structure that came out and say, that's wrong, let me reconsider.

With AlphaFold 2 we decided the whole thing should be end to end, and the network should reason directly about geometry. A few ideas came out of that. The first is what we called the Evoformer, where you have two representations, the MSA and a pair representation, and they talk to each other continually. The pair representation gets updated by attention that is aware of the triangle inequality, so if you know the relationship between residues i and j, and j and k, the network has an architectural bias toward keeping i and k consistent with that. That sounds like a small thing, but it is essentially the network learning to do geometric reasoning on a graph rather than treating distances as independent predictions.

The second idea is the structure module, where we represent every residue as a rigid frame, a rotation and a translation, and the network directly places those frames in three dimensions. The attention there, invariant point attention, is designed so that the geometry is equivariant, meaning that if you rotate the input you rotate the output and nothing else changes. And then we recycle: we take the predicted structure, feed it back in, and let the network refine its own answer. That iterative refinement turned out to matter a great deal.

And then on the training side, the thing people underestimate is self-distillation. We trained on the PDB, used the model to predict structures for a large set of sequences from UniRef, kept the confident ones, and trained again on that. The model's own confidence estimate, the pLDDT, was good enough that it could act as a filter, and that gave us roughly an order of magnitude more effective training data. Add in the FAPE loss, which is a frame-aligned point error so the loss itself is invariant to global rigid motions, plus the auxiliary losses on the distogram and the masked MSA, and you have a system where every piece was designed around the physics of the problem.

So when I say it was a large advance, I mean it in a qualitative sense. AlphaFold 1 could tell you roughly what a fold looked like. AlphaFold 2 could tell you where the atoms were, often within an angstrom or so, and more importantly it could tell you when it did not know. That second part, the calibrated confidence, is what made it a tool biologists could actually trust and use.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change was that we stopped treating structure prediction as a sequence of separate problems and built a system that could learn how those problems fit together. With AlphaFold 1, the neural network predicted things like distances between residues, and then a separate optimization procedure tried to find a structure consistent with those predictions. That was powerful, but it put a boundary between what the network learned and what we ultimately wanted it to do.

With AlphaFold 2, the network produces the structure directly, and we can train through that process. That changes the question from “How accurately can you predict these intermediate quantities?” to “Can you learn the computations that give you the right three-dimensional structure?”

The architecture makes that practical. We have representations of the sequence alignment and of relationships between pairs of residues, and those representations repeatedly exchange information. Then the structure module reasons explicitly in three dimensions. So we’re giving the network useful ways to think about the problem without prescribing every step of the solution.

Recycling is another part of that: the model can take its own prediction and use it to improve the next prediction. And the training matters enormously, including using predictions on sequences without experimental structures as additional training data.

What makes it a large advance, to me, is how those pieces work together. It isn’t just a larger network or one clever attention mechanism. It’s a system in which evolutionary information, geometric reasoning, and learning the final task are much more closely connected.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change was that we stopped treating structure prediction as a sequence of separate problems. In AlphaFold 1, the neural network predicted things like distances between residues, and then a separate optimization procedure tried to build a structure consistent with those predictions. That was useful, but it put a boundary between what the network learned and the structure we actually wanted.

With AlphaFold 2, we could train the system end to end to produce coordinates. The network could learn representations that were useful for building a structure, rather than only for predicting an intermediate quantity we had chosen.

The other big part was how information moved through the network. We had a representation of the multiple sequence alignment and a representation of relationships between pairs of residues, and we allowed those to communicate repeatedly. So evolutionary information could inform a hypothesis about structure, and that hypothesis could influence how the network interpreted the evolutionary information. The structure module then brought three-dimensional geometry directly into that computation.

Recycling was another important ingredient: taking the network’s prediction and feeding it back in so it could refine it. And on the training side, using predictions on sequences without experimental structures gave us a way to learn from much more data.

So I wouldn’t attribute the advance to one clever layer. It was the combination of an architecture that let the relevant information interact, a geometric way to produce structures, and training that made all those pieces work together. That changed what the system could learn.
